strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: continual unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models.
Provides a systematic empirical study showing that sequential unlearning leads to utility collapse and cumulative parameter drift.
Proposes a suite of add-on regularizers (L1/L2, SelFT, model merging) and a gradient-projection method, demonstrating improved retention in experiments.
Offers a theoretical bound linking parameter drift to retention loss via Taylor expansion, and provides empirical curvature estimates.
Well-motivated and structured, with clear identification of a gap in existing unlearning literature.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confounded: unlearning accuracy (UA) may remain high simply because generated images degrade, not because unlearning is selective. No image quality metrics (e.g., FID, CLIP score) or human evaluation are reported to ensure unlearned concepts are removed without destroying image content.

Potential mischaracterization of ConAbl: if ConAbl only optimizes text embeddings (as in the original work), then the parameter drift analysis and gradient projection on W_K/W_V are invalid for this method. The paper does not clarify whether ConAbl is adapted to update model weights.

Gradient projection formulation is mathematically imprecise: it treats the gradient with respect to W_K/W_V as a vector, but these gradients are matrices. It is unclear how the projection onto a subspace of text embeddings is applied to matrix gradients (e.g., flattening or row-wise projection), and Lemma 7.1 only holds for vectors.

Lack of quantitative results: the main text relies on small figures without exact numbers, error bars, or statistical significance tests, making it difficult to assess the magnitude and reliability of improvements.

Limited baselines: only ConAbl and EraseDiff are evaluated; other popular concept-erasure methods (e.g., ESD, SALUN, CA) and continual learning baselines (e.g., EWC, GPM) are missing, weakening the claim that the proposed regularizers are strong baselines.

Hyperparameters (λ for L1/L2, k% for SelFT and TIES, number M and selection of auxiliary concepts, similarity threshold) are not specified or ablated, raising reproducibility concerns. Auxiliary concept generation depends on an LLM without details.

Limited novelty: the add-on regularizers are standard adaptations from continual learning, and the gradient-projection method is a simple orthogonal projection similar to existing techniques (e.g., GPM). The theoretical analysis is a straightforward Taylor bound.

The benchmark is only an extension of UnlearnCanvas with sequential orders; no new dataset is released, and experiments are limited to one diffusion model (Stable Diffusion) and one dataset, limiting generality.

Model merging requires storing all independently unlearned models, which scales linearly with the number of requests; memory and compute trade-offs are not discussed, undermining practical efficiency claims.

The theoretical support is weak: the bound includes an unestimated gradient norm term, and the empirical curvature estimate does not validate the bound for sequential unlearned models. No guarantee that projected gradients still effectively unlearn the target concept.

strengths: Addresses a timely and realistic problem: continual/sequential unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models, which is underexplored compared with one-shot concept erasure.
Provides a benchmark/protocol extending UnlearnCanvas with sequential style/object unlearning and separates in-domain and cross-domain retention metrics.
Empirically demonstrates that ConAbl and EraseDiff suffer severe utility collapse under sequential unlearning while remaining effective in the simultaneous setting.
Offers a useful diagnostic perspective by linking retention degradation to cumulative parameter drift from the pre-trained weights.

Explores several practical add-on regularizers (L1/L2, selective fine-tuning, model merging, and semantic gradient projection) and shows they can improve retention, with gradient projection especially improving in-domain retention.
weaknesses: The central proposed method, gradient projection, is technically unclear or dimensionally inconsistent: the gradient is taken with respect to W_K/W_V matrices, but the projection and Lemma 7.1 treat it as a vector in the text-embedding space. It is not specified how to project matrix gradients, nor how this interacts with the rest of the unlearning parameters.

Missing critical ablation: there is no comparison against projection onto random subspaces, unrelated-concept subspaces, or all concept directions. Without this, the gains cannot be attributed to semantic awareness rather than a generic constraint on W_K/W_V updates.

Evaluation is too narrow: only one fine-tuned Stable Diffusion checkpoint and UnlearnCanvas are used, likely with a single random unlearning sequence per setting, no multiple orders/seeds, and no confidence intervals. Only ConAbl and EraseDiff are evaluated; other unlearning methods and stronger continual-learning baselines are absent.

The metrics are insufficient for the utility-collapse claim. UA can remain high simply because a degraded/noisy model fails to produce the target concept, and there is no FID, CLIP score, image-quality measure, or human evaluation. Retention accuracy alone does not establish that generated images are meaningful.

The theoretical analysis is largely a standard Taylor expansion plus Cauchy-Schwarz bound and only states that retention loss changes with parameter drift. It does not explain why sequential unlearning fails more than simultaneous unlearning, nor does it justify the semantic projection method.

Reproducibility is limited: key hyperparameters (regularization strength, top-k percentages, number M of auxiliary concepts, LLM generation/filtering details, projection implementation) are not reported, and there is no code or compute/efficiency quantification despite the claimed efficiency-utility trade-off.

Several add-on regularizers are off-the-shelf adaptations from continual learning/model merging (L1/L2, SelFT, TIES), and the empirical study does not provide enough rigorous evidence to support the broad claim that it establishes a fundamental challenge and principled solution.

The paper overclaims relative to the evidence: the claim that semantic awareness is crucial is supported mainly by a correlation for one unlearned concept, and the gradient-projection results are shown mostly as aggregate plots without raw numerical results or detailed ablations.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: continual unlearning in text-to-image diffusion models, where requests arrive sequentially rather than all at once.
Introduces a benchmark extending UnlearnCanvas for continual style and object unlearning, with clear metrics UA, RA-I, and RA-C.
Systematically demonstrates that existing unlearning methods (ConAbl, EraseDiff) suffer rapid retention collapse under sequential unlearning, and links this to cumulative parameter drift.
Provides a theoretical intuition via a Taylor-expansion bound relating retention loss change to parameter drift, supported by empirical Hessian estimates.
Studies several practical add-on regularizers (L1/L2, SelFT, TIES model merging) and a semantic-aware gradient-projection method, showing they improve retention and are compatible with each other.
The paper is well-written, clearly structured, and offers useful insights and open directions for a new research direction.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark (UnlearnCanvas) and one model checkpoint; there is no evaluation on larger diffusion models or multiple datasets, limiting generalization.

No image-quality or prompt-alignment metrics (e.g., FID, CLIP score) or human evaluation are reported, so high UA may reflect degraded generation rather than clean concept removal; utility is only indirectly captured by classifier-based RA.

Baselines are narrow: only ConAbl and EraseDiff are compared, with no other recent unlearning methods (e.g., ESD, UCE) or standard continual-learning regularizers (EWC, SI, MAS) despite the regularization perspective.

Insufficient ablations and hyperparameter sensitivity: choices of L1/L2 weight, SelFT top-k%, TIES merge k%, and especially the number, selection, and similarity threshold of auxiliary concepts for gradient projection are not analyzed.

The gradient-projection method is only applied to cross-attention W_K and W_V; the justification for restricting to these parameters is weak, and there is no analysis of whether unlearning accuracy (UA) is preserved when target and auxiliary concepts are close.

The theoretical analysis is a straightforward Taylor/Cauchy-Schwarz upper bound; it does not prove that cumulative drift causes the collapse, only that retention loss can be bounded by drift, and the Hessian estimate is rough and not tightly connected to the sequential vs. simultaneous gap.

The claim that semantic awareness is crucial is supported mainly by one unlearning target ('Abstractionism') and a correlation plot; broader evidence across many concepts and sequence orders is missing.

Efficiency and scalability are not quantified in the main text: model merging requires storing and merging an increasing number of independent models, and simultaneous retraining costs are not compared quantitatively with sequential/add-on methods.
Reproducibility is limited: no code/data release is mentioned, auxiliary concept generation via an LLM is not fully specified, and there are no confidence intervals or multiple random sequence runs.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: continual unlearning (CU) for text-to-image diffusion models, motivated by realistic sequential removal requests.
Provides the first systematic study and benchmark for CU in text-to-image generation, extending UnlearnCanvas with style- and object-level sequences and metrics UA, RA-I, and RA-C.

Clearly diagnoses the failure mode of existing methods as cumulative parameter drift and semantic interference, supported by empirical drift analysis, text-embedding similarity correlation, and a Taylor-expansion bound.

Proposes and evaluates several plug-and-play regularizers (L1/L2, SelFT, TIES merging) and a semantic-aware gradient-projection method, showing consistent improvements across multiple unlearning methods and settings (styles, objects, celebrity, SDXL).
Writing is clear, figures are informative, and the paper offers useful practical insights (e.g., anchor-driven updates, all-or-nothing erasure, drift intrinsic to sequential unlearning).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: most regularizers are adaptations of existing continual learning/model merging techniques, and the gradient-projection method is a simple orthogonal projection with a trivial first-order invariance lemma. The main contribution is empirical rather than a new algorithm.

Theoretical analysis is shallow: the Taylor-expansion bound is standard and does not fully explain why sequential unlearning accumulates more drift than simultaneous unlearning; the empirical curvature validation is limited.

Missing baselines: despite framing the work as a regularization perspective, there is no comparison to established continual learning regularizers such as EWC, SI, MAS, or A-GEM, nor to replay-based methods. The simultaneous-retraining baseline is useful but not sufficient.

Evaluation limitations: the main experiments rely heavily on one benchmark (UnlearnCanvas) with a single random sequence and no reported variance or error bars; FID/CLIP and human evaluation are mostly absent for the core style/object settings, and retention remains far from perfect despite claims of substantial restoration.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, and key hyperparameters (e.g., lambda, k%, number of auxiliary concepts, similarity threshold) and implementation details are missing or only partially described.

Gradient projection is under-specified and unablated: sensitivity to the number and selection of auxiliary concepts, applicability beyond W_K/W_V, and potential degradation of unlearning accuracy are not thoroughly analyzed.
Model merging requires storing all independently unlearned models and may not scale to long sequences; memory and compute trade-offs are not fully evaluated.

Several references appear corrupted or nonsensical (e.g., malformed author lists, a 2026 arXiv citation, and titles such as "A model for the neural network"), raising concerns about scholarship and citation accuracy.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: continual unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models, where erasure requests arrive sequentially.
Provides a broad empirical study across multiple settings (styles, objects, celebrities), architectures (Stable Diffusion, SDXL), and unlearning methods (ConAbl, SculpMem, ESD).
Identifies and measures a clear failure mode—utility collapse under sequential unlearning—and links it empirically to cumulative parameter drift relative to the pre-trained model.
Proposes several plug-in regularizers (L1/L2 update penalties, selective fine-tuning, model merging, and semantic-aware gradient projection) that are compatible with existing unlearning methods.
The gradient-projection method improves in-domain retention and can be combined with other regularizers for further gains, as shown in several experiments.
The paper is generally well organized, with a clear problem statement, benchmark protocol, and extensive appendix containing additional results.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core idea of regularizing parameter drift is standard in continual learning, and the proposed gradient projection is closely related to existing null-space/gradient-projection methods (e.g., A-GEM, GPM). No comparison to these continual-learning baselines is provided.

The theoretical analysis is shallow: the Taylor-expansion bound is standard and potentially vacuous for large parameter drift, does not explain why sequential and simultaneous unlearning differ, and does not provide guarantees for the proposed regularizers. The empirical Hessian estimation is weak and not reported in enough detail.

Technical ambiguity in the gradient-projection method: gradients with respect to W_K and W_V are matrices, but the paper describes projecting a gradient vector onto the orthogonal complement of a text-embedding subspace. The operation is not clearly defined for matrix-valued gradients, and Lemma 7.1 only covers vector updates.

Insufficient ablation for the semantic-aware component: the paper does not compare against random auxiliary concepts, random projections, or varying the number/similarity threshold of auxiliary concepts. Thus the claimed benefit of semantic awareness is not causally isolated.

Evaluation lacks important baselines: no comparisons to established continual-learning regularizers such as EWC, SI, MAS, or replay/rehearsal methods, nor to other efficient continual-unlearning strategies. The simultaneous retraining baseline is an expensive oracle, not a practical alternative.

Reproducibility is limited: key hyperparameters (regularization strength λ, top-k%, number of auxiliary concepts M, similarity thresholds, LLM prompt details), compute requirements, and training seeds are largely missing. No code or benchmark release is mentioned.

Experimental rigor could be stronger: results appear to be from single training runs without error bars or statistical significance tests; metrics rely on classifier-based accuracy, with limited image-quality or human evaluation on the main benchmark.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: “first systematic study” may overclaim, “semantic awareness is crucial” is supported mainly by correlation, and model merging requires storing and merging all independently unlearned models with unanalyzed memory/compute costs.

The paper reads more like a benchmark/empirical report than a top-tier conference paper; the main insight—sequential updates cause drift and regularization helps—is expected from prior continual-learning literature, and the proposed solutions are plug-in heuristics rather than principled continual-unlearning algorithms.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: continual unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models, motivated by realistic sequential unlearning requests.
Provides a systematic empirical study and benchmark extension of UnlearnCanvas with style- and object-level unlearning sequences, evaluating unlearning accuracy and in-domain/cross-domain retention.

Identifies cumulative parameter drift as a key cause of utility collapse in sequential unlearning and demonstrates that generic add-on regularizers (L1/L2, selective fine-tuning, model merging) can mitigate it.

Proposes a semantic-aware gradient-projection method to preserve concepts semantically close to the unlearning target, showing improvements in in-domain retention and compatibility with other regularizers.
Includes extensive experiments across style, object, and celebrity erasure; multiple unlearning methods (ConAbl, SculpMem, ESD); and an additional SDXL setting, supporting generality of the findings.
weaknesses: The gradient-projection formulation appears dimensionally inconsistent: gradients with respect to W_K and W_V are matrices, while the projection is defined for vectors in the text-embedding space. The correct operation likely requires right-multiplication by (I - P_S), but the paper uses left-multiplication. As written, the method and Lemma 7.1 are unclear and potentially invalid.

The theoretical analysis is a straightforward Taylor expansion bound and offers limited insight into why sequential unlearning drifts more than simultaneous unlearning; the empirical Hessian validation is weak and does not deeply support the central claim.

Main style and object evaluations rely primarily on classifier accuracy for UA and RA, without quantitative image-quality metrics (e.g., FID or CLIP score) or human evaluation. Degradation is shown qualitatively but not fully quantified in the main benchmark.

The auxiliary concepts used for gradient projection are described only as 'generated by an LLM and filtered by text-embedding similarity,' with no details on number, selection criteria, or sensitivity, harming reproducibility and principled design.
Evaluation uses a single random sequence of 12 concepts (or few sequences) without reporting multiple sequence orders or random seeds, leaving robustness to request order unclear.

Comparisons are limited to a few unlearning methods in the main text; broader baselines from the concept-erasure literature are not systematically evaluated, making the empirical positioning somewhat narrow.
No code or implementation details are provided for reproducibility, and the reference list contains incomplete or corrupted entries, which affects clarity and verifiability.
